message.content:
Let the projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(P\) be
\[
\mathbf{v}=p\mathbf{b}+q\mathbf{c}.
\]
Since \(\mathbf{v}\) is the orthogonal projection of \(\mathbf{a}\) onto \(P\), the vector \(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{v}\) is perpendicular to both \(\mathbf{b}\) and \(\mathbf{c}\). Thus,
\[
(\mathbf{a}-p\mathbf{b}-q\mathbf{c})\cdot \mathbf{b}=0
\]
and
\[
(\mathbf{a}-p\mathbf{b}-q\mathbf{c})\cdot \mathbf{c}=0.
\]

Given:
\[
\mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{b}=\frac15,\qquad \mathbf{a}\cdot \mathbf{c}=\frac16,\qquad \mathbf{b}\cdot \mathbf{c}=\cos 60^\circ=\frac12.
\]
Also \(\mathbf{b}\cdot\mathbf{b}=1\) and \(\mathbf{c}\cdot\mathbf{c}=1\).

From the first dot product equation:
\[
\frac15-p-\frac12 q=0
\]
so
\[
p+\frac12 q=\frac15.
\]

From the second:
\[
\frac16-\frac12 p-q=0
\]
so
\[
\frac12 p+q=\frac16.
\]

Solve the system:
\[
p+\frac12 q=\frac15,
\]
\[
\frac12 p+q=\frac16.
\]
Multiplying the first by 2 gives
\[
2p+q=\frac25.
\]
The second gives
\[
p+2q=\frac13.
\]
Solving,
\[
p=\frac{7}{45},\qquad q=\frac{4}{45}.
\]

Therefore the ordered pair is
\[
\left(\frac{7}{45},\frac{4}{45}\right).
\]

The answer is \(\left(\frac{7}{45},\frac{4}{45}\right)\).
